items.text: Pop's first mix put most of the instruments on one side of the stereo and the vocals on the other.
items.why: Recording: 'his botched first attempt mixed most of the instruments into one stereo channel and the vocals into the other'.

items.text: 7 February 1973
items.why: Infobox 'Released: February 7, 1973'.

items.text: September to October 1972, CBS Studios, London
items.why: Infobox 'Recorded: September–October 1972', 'Studios: CBS , London'; Recording 'recorded at CBS Studios in London ... from September 10 to October 6, 1972'.

items.text: David Bowie, Iggy Pop
items.why: Infobox 'Producers: David Bowie Iggy Pop'. (The body says Pop produced the sessions and Bowie did the mix.)

items.text: Columbia
items.why: Infobox 'Label: Columbia'.

items.text: The first two Stooges albums had little commercial success, and the group had split up.
items.why: Background: 'released to little commercial success, the Stooges were in disarray: the band had officially broken up'.

items.text: Pop's heroin addiction was getting worse when David Bowie stepped in.
items.why: Background: 'Iggy Pop's heroin addiction was escalating prior to the intervention of David Bowie'.

items.text: Pop signed with Columbia as a solo artist and moved to London to make an album with guitarist James Williamson.
items.why: Background: 'Having signed on as a solo artist to Columbia Records, Pop relocated to London, where he was to write and record an album with James Williamson'.

items.text: When they could not find a suitable rhythm section in England, Williamson suggested bringing in Ron and Scott Asheton, both former Stooges.
items.why: Background: 'When they failed to find a suitable English rhythm section, Williamson suggested that former Stooges Ron Asheton and Scott Asheton fly over'.

items.text: The band reformed under the name Iggy and the Stooges, and the elder Asheton, its founding guitarist, reluctantly agreed to switch to bass.
items.why: Background: 'the band's reformation under the new name of "Iggy and the Stooges". Although he was the band's founding guitarist, the elder Asheton reluctantly agreed to switch to electric bass.'

items.text: Staff engineer Mike Ross-Trevor worked on the recording.
items.why: Recording: 'recorded at CBS Studios in London with staff engineer Mike Ross-Trevor'.

items.text: Pop said Columbia insisted on a ballad for each side of the record: "Gimme Danger" and "I Need Somebody".
items.why: Recording: 'Pop said that Columbia executives insisted on two ballads, one for each side of the album: "Gimme Danger" and "I Need Somebody".'

items.text: Because the budget was tight, Bowie reworked seven of the eight songs in one day at Western Sound Recorders in Los Angeles, and Pop kept his own mix of "Search and Destroy".
items.why: Recording: 'Due to budgetary constraints, Bowie remixed the other seven songs in a single day at Los Angeles' Western Sound Recorders' and Pop 'insisted that his own mix for "Search and Destroy" be retained'; Lead gives eight songs.

items.text: Bowie later recalled that on some songs only three of the 24 tracks were used, and that he often raised and lowered the vocal.
items.why: Recording, Bowie quote: 'Out of 24 tracks there were just three tracks that were used ... we just pushed the vocal up and down a lot. On at least four or five songs'. Attributed correctly, but the pack adds that Morgan Neville's 2010 documentary showed each instrument was on its own track, 'suggesting that Bowie was either mistaken'; the notes leave that correction out.

items.text: Columbia dropped the band after roughly a year of touring, and the group split up in February 1974.
items.why: Marketing and sales: 'The group continued touring for about a year, but Columbia dropped their contract ... The Stooges broke up in February 1974.'

items.text: While on day release from rehab, Pop recorded Kill City with Williamson.
items.why: Marketing and sales: 'rehab at the UCLA Neuropsychiatric Institute, during which he would record the album Kill City with Williamson whilst on day release'.

items.text: In 1993 Bomp Records released a selection of the original mixes as Rough Power.
items.why: Alternate mixes: 'In 1993, a selection of these original mixes was released by Bomp Records as Rough Power.'

items.text: In 1996 Columbia invited Pop to remix the whole record for CD, and the remixed edition came out on 22 April 1997.
items.why: Alternate mixes: 'In 1996, Columbia Records "invited" Pop to remix the entire album for re-release on CD ... The remixed edition was released on April 22, 1997.' The pack's scare quotes (he says they would have remixed it anyway) are dropped, a lost nuance rather than an error.

items.text: In 2012 both mixes were remastered for a double LP released for Record Store Day, and in 2023 they were remastered again for the album's fiftieth anniversary.
items.why: Alternate mixes: 'Pop and Bowie's mixes were both remastered in 2012 for a Record Store Day double LP'; 'In 2023, both mixes of the album were once again remastered ... to commemorate its fiftieth anniversary.'

items.text: Pop says Bowie ran this guitar through a Time Cube, a bent plastic tube that makes the sound hit you with an echo.
items.why: Recording, Pop quote: 'a Time Cube ... a big plastic tube with a couple of bends in it -- and when the sound came out the other end, it sort of shot at you like an echo effect. He used that on the guitar in "Gimme Danger"'. Title matches the track list.

items.where: listen_for: Your Pretty Face Is Going to Hell
items.text: Pop says Bowie also ran the drums through the Time Cube, wanting the drummer to sound like someone beating a log.
items.why: Recording: 'and on the drums in "Your Pretty Face Is Going To Hell". His concept was, "You're so primitive, your drummer should sound like he's beating a log!"' Title matches the track list (capitalisation only).

items.text: Robert Christgau says the celeste can finally be heard on this track in Pop's remix.
items.why: Alternate mixes, Christgau on the 1997 edition: 'Plus you can finally hear the celeste on "Penetration"'. Title matches the track list.

missed: How it sounds: the lead and Musical style say it left the 'groove-ridden, feel-based songs' of the first two albums for a more anthemic hard rock approach driven by new guitarist Williamson, who co-wrote all eight songs with Pop. Also that the 1997 remix is famously extreme in loudness (RMS of -4 dB, deliberately in the red), which matters for which version a listener hears.
